title: SQL Database in Microsoft Fabric: Operational OLTP Meets the Lakehouse
summary: SQL database in Fabric is a fully managed transactional database engine built on the same SQL Database Engine as Azure SQL Database. It automatically replicates data to OneLake in near-real time, enabling translytical patterns where OLTP writes and analytical reads co-exist without contention — all governed by Microsoft Entra ID and managed under a single Fabric capacity.
body_md:
## What Is SQL Database in Fabric?

SQL database in Fabric is a developer-oriented transactional database engine that shares the same underlying SQL Database Engine as Azure SQL Database, making it the designated home for OLTP workloads within the Fabric platform [S1]. It is not a separate product bolted on — it is a first-class Fabric item that lives inside a workspace, billed through the workspace's capacity, and governed by the same identity and security controls that apply to the rest of the platform.

The key idea is that transactional workloads have always needed separation from analytical workloads: heavy reads kill write latency, and write storms ruin query plans. SQL database in Fabric solves this at the architectural level rather than through manual tuning. By continuously replicating every write into OneLake, it creates a clean boundary between the two traffic types without forcing application teams to maintain a separate ETL pipeline.

For practitioners already running Azure SQL Database, the learning curve is minimal. The engine is the same, the tooling (SSMS, Azure Data Studio, SqlPackage) connects the same way, and T-SQL dialects are compatible. What changes is that the database now sits inside the Fabric ecosystem rather than standing alone.

## How Automatic Replication and the Analytics Endpoint Work

When a SQL database is created in Fabric, the platform automatically and continuously replicates its data into OneLake in near-real time, converting it to Parquet format so that downstream analytical services — Spark, notebooks, Power BI, data engineering pipelines — can consume it without any manual export step [S1].

Provisioning a SQL database in a Fabric workspace also automatically creates a companion SQL analytics endpoint, giving read-only analytical access to the replicated OneLake data without affecting the transactional workload [S1]. This endpoint appears alongside the database in the workspace and is addressable with standard T-SQL, so existing BI tools and query tools connect to it without modification.

*Inference:* The combination of automatic replication and the auto-created analytics endpoint means that the path from an operational write to an analytical read requires zero hand-coded integration steps — the infrastructure wires itself together at provisioning time.

![SQL database in Fabric, translytical](/content/diagrams/sql-database-translytical.svg)

Because the replicated OneLake data is stored as Delta tables, a SQL analytics endpoint on one database can join data from other Fabric items — warehouses, mirrored databases, or other SQL databases — using standard three-part T-SQL naming, enabling cross-database federated queries without data movement [S1]. A single analytical query can therefore reach operational data from multiple SQL databases alongside historical warehouse data, all in one SELECT statement.

## Translytical Architecture: Separating Writes from Reads

SQL database in Fabric enables translytical application patterns by separating write traffic (through the transactional engine) from read/analytics traffic (through the SQL analytics endpoint backed by OneLake), eliminating contention between the two workloads [S1].

In practice, this means an application's INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE statements hit the transactional engine directly, while Power BI dashboards, Spark jobs, and ad-hoc analysts connect exclusively to the analytics endpoint. Neither side is aware of the other's load. The translytical pattern also avoids the operational complexity of CDC pipelines, replication slots, or scheduled data exports — the platform handles synchronisation continuously in the background.

This architecture suits a broad range of scenarios: e-commerce order systems where the same data drives both checkout and real-time sales reporting, IoT ingestion pipelines that need transactional guarantees alongside time-series analytics, and SaaS applications that want their tenants' operational data visible in Fabric without manual replication.

## Automatic Tuning and Autonomous Index Management

The database ships with automatic tuning enabled by default, including automatic index creation, so routine index management is handled autonomously rather than requiring manual DBA intervention [S1]. The engine monitors query patterns, identifies missing indexes, creates candidates, and verifies that the created index genuinely improves performance — reverting the change if it does not.

*Inference:* For teams without a dedicated DBA, this feature dramatically reduces the operational overhead of running a production transactional database. It does not replace deliberate schema design, but it catches many common indexing omissions that would otherwise go unnoticed until query performance degrades.

## AI and Vector Search

SQL database supports vector data types and integrates with Azure OpenAI and orchestration frameworks such as LangChain and Semantic Kernel, positioning it as a store for Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and semantic search workloads inside Fabric [S1].

For AI application teams, this means the same database that holds transactional records can also store and search vector embeddings — product descriptions, document chunks, user profile representations — without managing a separate vector database. Queries can combine structured SQL predicates with approximate nearest-neighbour vector similarity in a single query.

*Inference:* Keeping vectors co-located with their source records simplifies joins, reduces data movement, and cuts down on the number of services an AI application needs to operate. This is particularly useful for RAG patterns where retrieved context must be enriched with metadata from transactional records.

## Security and Identity

### Entra-Only Authentication

Authentication to a SQL database in Fabric is exclusively via Microsoft Entra ID; SQL authentication is not supported. A user, service principal, or group must hold at least the Read item permission on the database in Fabric before any connection succeeds [S1].

This is a deliberate design choice that eliminates a common attack surface: shared SQL logins with static passwords. Every principal connecting to the database must have a live Entra identity, and access can be revoked at the identity layer. Service accounts should use service principals or managed identities, which support secret rotation and short-lived tokens without application changes.

### Fine-Grained Access Controls

Security features include row-level security (RLS), object-level security (OLS), workspace-level customer-managed keys, and SQL auditing, bringing enterprise-grade access control and compliance capabilities to the transactional database inside Fabric [S1].

RLS allows a single table to serve multiple tenants or user roles with predicate-based row filtering applied at the engine, invisible to the application layer. OLS restricts which columns or objects different principals can read, useful for keeping PII fields out of reach for analyst roles. Customer-managed keys extend the workspace-level encryption model down to the SQL database, satisfying compliance requirements that mandate customer control over encryption material. SQL auditing writes a durable log of all connections and queries, supporting forensic and regulatory obligations.

## Capacity, Billing, and Resource Sharing

SQL database in Fabric does not map to Azure SQL elastic pools; instead, a single Fabric capacity spans multiple Fabric SQL databases across different workspaces, consolidating billing and providing resource sharing analogous to elastic pools while maintaining workspace-level security isolation [S1].

This model changes how teams should think about cost. Rather than provisioning and paying for each database individually, teams purchase Fabric capacity (in CUs) and allocate databases to workspaces that sit under that capacity. A spike in one database draws from shared capacity headroom; when the spike passes, the headroom returns to the pool. Workspace-level boundaries ensure that data and permissions remain isolated even though the underlying compute and storage billing is consolidated.

*Inference:* For organisations running dozens of small operational databases — one per business unit or per SaaS tenant — this model can reduce administrative overhead significantly compared to managing individual Azure SQL elastic pool configurations.

## DevOps, CI/CD, and Migration

Database portability is handled via SqlPackage, which supports .bacpac import/export and .dacpac schema deployments, enabling migration between Azure SQL Database and Fabric SQL database and supporting CI/CD-style incremental schema changes through SQL projects [S1].

This means existing Azure SQL migration tooling and deployment pipelines carry over directly. Teams using SQL Server Data Tools (SSDT), SQL projects in VS Code, or GitHub Actions workflows for schema drift detection can adopt Fabric SQL database without rewriting their deployment automation. .dacpac deployments handle incremental schema changes safely by generating a diff script rather than dropping and recreating objects.

*Inference:* The .bacpac path is also the natural migration route for teams moving off Azure SQL Database into Fabric: export the .bacpac from Azure SQL, import it into a Fabric SQL database, update connection strings, and the transactional tier is migrated. The analytical tier — the OneLake replica and analytics endpoint — provisions automatically on import.

## Best Practices

### Route the Right Traffic to the Right Endpoint

SQL database in Fabric enables translytical application patterns by keeping write traffic on the transactional engine and read/analytics traffic on the SQL analytics endpoint [S1]. Always configure application connection strings to point OLTP traffic at the primary database endpoint and analytical tools (Power BI, notebooks, ad-hoc queries) at the SQL analytics endpoint. Mixing heavy analytical reads into the transactional endpoint undermines the isolation the architecture provides.

### Lean on Automatic Tuning, but Design Schemas Deliberately

Automatic tuning handles reactive index management, but it works best on top of a well-considered schema [S1]. Normalise appropriately for the workload, choose clustered index keys that match the dominant access pattern, and let automatic tuning handle gaps discovered in production. Do not rely on automatic tuning to compensate for fundamentally misaligned table designs.

### Use Service Principals and Managed Identities for Automated Access

Because SQL authentication is not supported, any pipeline or application that needs non-interactive access must authenticate via Microsoft Entra ID [S1]. Register a service principal or use a managed identity for pipelines, Spark jobs, and Data Factory activities. Assign minimum-privilege Fabric item permissions plus only the necessary database-level roles.

### Use Cross-Database T-SQL for Federated Analytics Without ETL

The SQL analytics endpoint supports three-part T-SQL naming across Fabric items [S1]. Rather than building ETL pipelines to consolidate data from multiple SQL databases or warehouses, write cross-database SELECT statements that join directly across Delta-backed items. This avoids data duplication and keeps the analytical query close to the source of truth.

### Manage Schema Changes Through SQL Projects and .dacpac Deployments

SqlPackage and SQL projects support incremental schema deployments [S1]. Commit database schema to source control as a SQL project, generate .dacpac artifacts in CI, and deploy through a promotion pipeline. This gives version history, peer review, and rollback capability for every schema change, which is especially important when multiple application teams share a Fabric workspace.

## What Goes Wrong

### Sending Analytical Load to the Transactional Endpoint

The translytical pattern only works if analytical queries actually use the analytics endpoint [S1]. Teams that connect Power BI or Spark directly to the primary transactional endpoint (perhaps by reusing an existing connection string) will saturate the transactional engine with read I/O, defeating the isolation the architecture provides. Review all data consumer connection strings after provisioning and redirect any analytical consumers to the analytics endpoint.

### Attempting SQL Authentication

SQL authentication is not supported, so applications or pipelines that hardcode a SQL username and password will fail at connection time [S1]. This is a common failure mode when migrating from Azure SQL Database, where SQL authentication may have been the default. Audit all connection strings and service account configurations before migration, and replace static credentials with Entra-based identities.

### Assuming One-to-One Mapping with Azure SQL Elastic Pools

Fabric SQL databases do not correspond to Azure SQL elastic pools, and capacity is shared differently [S1]. Teams that plan resource allocation assuming per-database DTU/vCore limits will be surprised by the CU-based capacity model. Understand the Fabric capacity model before sizing: burst workloads draw from shared CU headroom, and sustained overuse results in throttling at the capacity level.

### Ignoring the Entra Permission Prerequisite

A principal must hold at least the Read item permission on the database Fabric item before any connection succeeds, regardless of database-level role assignments [S1]. Teams that grant database-level permissions but forget to assign the Fabric item permission will find that connections are rejected before they ever reach the database engine. Provision Fabric item permissions as part of the same deployment step as database role assignments.
